title_en: Ibadah — The Nature and Scope of Worship
summary: Ibadah (worship) in Islam is far broader than ritual acts. It encompasses every act done with sincere intention for the sake of Allah. Understanding its definition, conditions, and scope is foundational to Islamic practice.
content:
Ibadah (worship) is the reason humanity was created: 'I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me' (51:56). But what does worship mean in Islam? The scope of ibadah is one of the most important — and most misunderstood — concepts in the Islamic worldview.

## Definition

Ibn Taymiyyah (d. 728 AH) gave the most comprehensive classical definition: 'Ibadah is a comprehensive term for everything Allah loves and is pleased with — of statements and actions, whether inward or outward.'

This definition is significant in two ways:

1. **It is not limited to rituals.** Prayer, fasting, zakah, and hajj are acts of worship — but so is earning a lawful living with the intention of providing for one's family, speaking truthfully, being just in one's dealings, and showing kindness to a neighbour. Any permitted act performed with sincere intention for Allah's sake is worship.

2. **It is not limited to outward acts.** Inward states — love of Allah, fear of Allah, hope in Allah, trust (tawakkul), gratitude (shukr), repentance (tawbah), humility (khushu') — are themselves acts of worship. The heart's orientation is the root from which outward worship grows.

## The Two Conditions of Valid Worship (Pillars of Acceptance)

Classical scholars established that for any act to be accepted by Allah as worship, two conditions must be met — both are necessary, neither alone is sufficient:

### 1. Ikhlas — Sincerity
The act must be done purely for Allah alone, free from riya (showing off) and worldly motivations. Allah says: 'And they were not commanded except to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion' (98:5). An outwardly correct act done for human praise has no value as worship before Allah; it may earn worldly recognition, but it has missed the point entirely.

### 2. Ittiba' — Following the Prophet (peace be upon him)
The act must be done in the manner the Prophet brought. An act done sincerely but in a way not established by the Sunnah is bid'ah (innovation) and is not accepted: 'Whoever introduces into this matter of ours something that is not from it will have it rejected' (Bukhari 2697, Muslim 1718). Sincerity without correctness, and correctness without sincerity, are both insufficient.

## Categories of Worship

Scholars categorise acts of worship to show the breadth of the concept:

**Ritual worship ('ibadah shar'iyyah):** The established rites — salah, zakah, sawm, hajj, dhikr, du'a, reciting the Quran, making tawbah.

**Worship of the heart:** Love of Allah, fear of Him (khawf), hope in Him (raja'), reliance upon Him (tawakkul), awe of His greatness (khashyah), repentance (inabah).

**Worship through limbs:** All permitted acts done for Allah — feeding the poor, maintaining family ties, being just in business, abstaining from the forbidden.

**Du'a as worship:** The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Du'a is worship' (Abu Dawud 1479 — sahih). This is why directing du'a to other than Allah is shirk: du'a is an act of worship, and worship belongs only to Allah.

## The Scope of 'Ubudiyyah (Servitude)

The Arabic term 'ubudiyyah (servitude/slavery to Allah) is the highest description of the Muslim's relationship to Allah. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is honoured in the Quran with this title at its greatest moments: 'Subhana alladhi asra bi-'abdihi' — 'Exalted is He who took His servant by night' (17:1).

To be a servant ('abd) of Allah is not degradation — it is the highest station, because servitude to Allah is the only servitude that liberates. The servant of Allah is free from the slavery of desire, status, fear of others, and the opinions of creation.

## Worship and Everyday Life

The Islamic worldview does not draw a sharp line between religious and secular life. A Muslim who works, eats, sleeps, and interacts with family — doing all of this in accordance with Allah's commands, with proper intention — is in a state of continuous worship. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Even your sexual relations with your spouse are a form of sadaqah (charity).' The companions asked: 'How can we fulfil our desire and be rewarded for it?' He replied: 'If he did it in a forbidden way, he would bear a sin. So if he does it in a permitted way, he receives a reward' (Muslim 1006).

This expansive vision of worship is the foundation of the Islamic concept of halal — permitted acts are elevated by intention. It transforms the entire life of the believer into an act of continuous devotion.
evidence_quran: Surah adh-Dhariyat 51:56 — 'I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me'
Surah al-Bayyinah 98:5 — 'And they were not commanded except to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion'
Surah al-Isra 17:1 — 'Exalted is He who took His servant by night...' (highest title: 'abd)
Surah al-Fatihah 1:5 — 'It is You we worship and You we ask for help'
Surah al-An'am 6:162 — 'Say: Indeed, my prayer, my rites of sacrifice, my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the worlds'
evidence_hadith: Bukhari 2697, Muslim 1718 — 'Whoever introduces into this matter of ours something that is not from it will have it rejected'
Muslim 1006 — on marital relations as sadaqah (charity) when done lawfully with intention
scholar_positions: Ibn Taymiyyah's definition of ibadah as 'everything Allah loves and is pleased with' is the standard reference in Athari-influenced scholarship. Ash'ari and Maturidi scholars agree on the core concept; differences lie in finer theological questions about how acts are evaluated, not on the breadth of the concept itself. All schools agree on the two conditions of ikhlas and ittiba'.
sources: Ibn Taymiyyah, al-'Ubudiyyah (dedicated treatise on servitude and worship)
Ibn al-Qayyim, Madarij al-Salikin (worship and its levels)
al-Nawawi, Sharh Muslim (commentary on worship-related hadith)
Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali, Jami' al-'Ulum wal-Hikam (commentary on the conditions of accepted deeds)
